sources.title: Juan Luna (Q28867), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Juan Luna', description 'Filipino painter, sculptor and political activist (1857-1899)', Korean label 후안 루나 (Korean Wikipedia article of the same title), instance of human, citizen of the Philippines, three birth-date claims (23, 24 and 25 October 1857) and death on 7 December 1899. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Emmanuelle Sinardet, 'Allegories de la defaite chez deux peintres philippins: Spoliarium (1884) de Juan Luna et Las virgenes cristianas expuestas al populacho (1884) de Felix Hidalgo', Crisol serie numerique no. 2 (Universite Paris Nanterre, 2018; peer-reviewed academic article, read in full from the open-access PDF, in French). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Spoliarium (422 x 767 cm) won the first gold medal at the 1884 Madrid national exhibition and is today the best-known painting of the Philippines; the review in the Gazette des Beaux-Arts called it the sensation of the exhibition and said the jury ratified the public's enthusiasm; Luna, aged 27, had already won a second medal in 1881 for The Death of Cleopatra; Philippine reformists of the Propaganda Movement read the dragged, stripped gladiators as an allegory of colonial rule, while the same movement sought Spanish sympathy. Independent academic reading of the painting's reception.

Eugenio Matibag, 'A Filipino Painter in Paris: Juan Luna in the Field of Cultural Production', Perspectives in the Arts and Humanities Asia 7(2), 2017, pp. 43-65 (peer-reviewed essay, Iowa State University; read in full from the open-access PDF). Scholarly biography of his Madrid, Rome and Paris years (1877-1893): training under Alejo Vera, the 1884 gold medal and the Medal of Honour he was denied, the Senate and Overseas Ministry commissions, the shift to commissioned portraits and miniatures to pay household costs, his hybrid academic-impressionist works and letters to Rizal, and, without softening, the 1892 killing of his wife and mother-in-law and his 1893 acquittal. Draws on earlier Luna scholarship (Pilar, Villegas, Aguilar Cruz, Reyes, Mojares) and on the 1893 trial pleading; frank about the violence and about official Philippine history's omission of it.

Blas Sierra de la Calle, 'Felix Resurreccion Hidalgo y Juan Luna y Novicio: obras en Ilustracion Artistica y La Ilustracion Espanola y Americana', Archivo Agustiniano 97 (2013) (scholarly article by an Augustinian archivist, in Spanish; the introduction, the short biography of Luna and the catalogue entries for Luna's cover portrait and the Spoliarium engraving were read). Gives Luna's life in outline (nautical school and pilot's licence 1874, dispute with the head of the Manila academy, lessons with Lorenzo Guerrero, Madrid 1877, Rome with Alejo Vera 1879-1884, Paris from 1884, the Senate commission of The Battle of Lepanto, a change from about 1890 to social-realist themes, return to the Philippines in 1894, arrest in 1896, diplomatic missions 1898-99, death in Hong Kong) and quotes the 1884 Ilustracion Artistica chronicle by Manuel Angelon; also identifies the cover portrait of issue no. 147 (20 October 1884) as 'Don Juan Luna y Novicio, autor de Spoliarium', engraver Saderns, photographer not named.

Ambeth R. Ocampo, 'Luna's pursuit of greatness', Philippine Daily Inquirer (14 June 2023; read in full). Column by the leading historian of the period: Luna's reputation rests on Spoliarium, the 1884 gold was the first of only three first-class medals for painting and the Medal of Honour was withheld; his first international recognition was the 1881 silver medal for The Death of Cleopatra; he won eight medals, five awards and a Spanish knighthood by 1904 and 'painted consistently, furiously' for the Medal of Honour that eluded him; Rizal's 1884 toast. Admiring but corrects the popular 'Olympic gold' reading.

Ruel S. De Vera, 'Long-lost Luna "greatest PH art find in history"', Philippine Daily Inquirer (11 June 2023; read in full). News report on the rediscovered painting Hymen, oh Hymenee!: painted on his honeymoon trip from Rome to Venice and finished most likely in 1887, kept in his Paris studio, submitted to the 1889 Exposition Universelle (the media pressed for him to be shown in the Spanish section, but he could not exhibit the paintings he wanted, so he sent this one), bronze medal there, lost after his death in 1899 and found in a European aristocratic family's collection. Exhibition-driven reporting based on the Ayala Museum and the auction-house owner.

Lance Spencer Yu, '"Painter as hero": How Juan Luna first awakened the Filipino spirit', Rappler (12 June 2023; read in full). Exhibition feature quoting Ayala Museum curators: the 1881 Death of Cleopatra, Spoliarium's 1884 gold medal, Hymen's 1889 bronze, Luna's mentor Alejo Vera, the observation that he did not speak of politics when he won, never became as vocal as Rizal and del Pilar but allied himself with Propaganda Movement members, and in 1899 served on delegations seeking recognition of the Philippine republic. Celebratory; shares the Ayala exhibition as its source.

R. C. Ladrido, 'Juan Luna: A painting rediscovered and murders recalled', VERA Files (27 September 2023; read in full). COUNTER-VOICE: reviews the Ayala exhibition and faults it for omitting his 1892 killing of his wife Paz Pardo de Tavera and mother-in-law Juliana Gorricho; summarises the account in Ruby Paredes's chapter in McCoy, An Anarchy of Families (1994): the shooting on 22 September 1892, Paz's death weeks later, his earlier beating of her and his demand for a duel, and the Seine assize court's acquittal on 8 February 1893. Also gives the 1886 marriage, the household's reliance on his mother-in-law's monthly money and the Ilustrado circle in Paris.

competitiveness.rationale: [src_luna_matibag, src_luna_sinardet, src_luna_sierra, src_luna_ocampo | 1881-1889 | scholarly essay, scholarly article, scholarly biography, historian's column] He repeatedly put his large canvases into the official competitions of his day: a second-class medal at the 1881 Madrid national exhibition for The Death of Cleopatra, a first-class medal there in 1884 for Spoliarium (he was not given the Medal of Honour, and Matibag records that the king told him he regretted this), a gold medal at the Paris Societe des Artistes Francais in 1886 (Matibag, citing Villegas) and the 1889 Paris Exposition Universelle. Matibag writes that he felt obliged to repeat the Spoliarium triumph, and Ocampo says he painted on in pursuit of the Medal of Honour that eluded him for the rest of his life. Most of the instances are medal outcomes and the motive rests on two interpretive remarks, so this is a moderate reading. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.56 to 64 / 0.52 because the pursuit of the Medal of Honour is one historian's sentence and the medals are outcomes, not behaviour. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered again to 62 / 0.50 because four of the five instances are prizes, which is outcome bias.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_luna_sierra, src_luna_matibag, src_luna_ocampo | 1869-1890 | scholarly biography, scholarly essay, historian's column] Sierra de la Calle traces a pilot's licence at 17, drawing at the Manila academy (he left after a dispute with its director), private lessons with Lorenzo Guerrero, the San Fernando academy in Madrid from 1877, and then study with Alejo Vera, whom he followed to Rome in 1879 and always called his master; the 1884 magazine chronicle he quotes says Luna took up drawing only about 1878 yet 'followed his career at a forced march'. Matibag adds that in Paris he worked at mastering Salon conventions and wrote to Rizal in 1888 and 1890 about open-air painting and the 'dissident salon'. The path is documented, but it is also the usual route of a painter of his time and the chronicle is a celebratory 1884 magazine piece. CONCENTRATION AND SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 to 60 / 0.46 because the training path is partly an occupational norm and the speed claim comes from a celebratory chronicle.

experimentation.rationale: [src_luna_matibag, src_luna_sierra | 1884-1892 | scholarly essay, scholarly biography] Matibag describes quasi-impressionist works made alongside academic commissions in the Paris years (the opera-box picture En el palco of 1884, seascapes and easel paintings of the 1890s) and quotes his May 1890 letter placing himself with the 'dissident salon' while rejecting colour divisionism; Sierra de la Calle says that from about 1890 he left the academic style and historical subjects for social-realist themes (El Trapero, Los Desheredados, Heroes anonimos, and Pueblo y Rey in 1892). Matibag stresses that he never fully committed to impressionism and was 'no heretic', so the lean is moderate. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 to 58 / 0.46 because the social-realist shift rests on one biographer's summary and describes subject matter more than method.

adaptability.rationale: [src_luna_matibag, src_luna_inq_hymen | 1884-1893 | scholarly essay, newspaper report] Matibag says that from 1884 he shuttled between Paris and Madrid painting commissioned portraits and moved from large canvases to miniatures and portraits to earn a living when prizes and commissions did not cover his family's rent; the Inquirer says that at the 1889 Exposition Universelle he was allowed to show in the Spanish section but could not exhibit the works he wanted and sent Hymen, oh Hymenee! instead, which won the bronze medal. Two instances, one from a single scholar and one from an exhibition news report, so a moderate score. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.48 to 58 / 0.42 because each instance rests on one account and the 1889 substitution is explained only as 'a variety of reasons'.

persistence.rationale: [src_luna_matibag, src_luna_ocampo | 1879-1899 | scholarly essay, historian's column] Matibag says that in Rome he went on producing paintings despite conditions of poverty, and Ocampo that he painted 'consistently, furiously' for the Medal of Honour that eluded him for the rest of his life. Both are one-sentence characterisations with no detailed episode, so this is an inference, not a documented pattern. CONCENTRATION CORRECTION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.46 strong_inference to 56 / 0.42 inference because neither source documents a specific setback and continuation.

portrait.source: Engraved portrait of Juan Luna, 'Don Juan Luna y Novicio, autor de Spoliarium', on the cover of La Ilustracion Artistica (Barcelona, Montaner y Simon), issue no. 147, 20 October 1884; engraver Saderns working from a photograph (photographer not named), as catalogued by Sierra de la Calle (Archivo Agustiniano 2013, entry no. 0010). Digitised in the Biblioteca Nacional de Espana, Hemeroteca Digital, and shown as a crop on Wikimedia Commons (1019 x 1330); this copy is the Commons crop downscaled to 766 x 1000, never upscaled. The printed caption is not visible in the crop; the sitter is identified by the holder-described cover, the 1884 issue that celebrates the Spoliarium gold medal, and the scholarly catalogue entry. The BNE item viewer sits behind a security check and could not be opened, so the item-level record was not read.

provenance.notes: Roster70. PORTRAIT PREFLIGHT: Stage B grade PLAUSIBLE (downgraded from strong); the lead (BNE Hemeroteca Digital cover of La Ilustracion Artistica, 20 Oct 1884) SURVIVED. Item record: the BNE viewer returns a security-check page (bot wall, not bypassed; recorded separately from any rights conflict), so the printed caption was not seen on the Commons crop; instead the cover, issue number (147), title, engraver (Saderns) and 'photographer not named' were confirmed in Sierra de la Calle's catalogue entry, and the BNE reuse rules were read (open, CC BY 4.0 or equivalent for public-domain Hemeroteca images, attribution wording quoted). Age path: published in Spain 20 Oct 1884, creators of unrecorded dates (an engraver after a photograph), so US public domain by pre-1931 publication; no holder contradiction found. Fallback not used: Commons 'Juan Luna.jpg' (studio photograph c.1885-90, Frick library record is a JavaScript page and could not be read). Kind likeness (engraving of a photograph of the sitter, made in his lifetime). IDENTITY: QID Q28867 verified live 2026-11-24 (human, label Juan Luna, 1857-1899). Region south_asia follows the Rizal precedent for the Philippines; era 19th_century (active 1877-1899); Korean name from the Wikidata ko label and Korean Wikipedia title. EVIDENCE: attribution is attributable (dated competitions, commissions and exhibitions; the Matibag and Sierra accounts are scholarly and the Sinardet article uses the 1884 press). Sparse 5-row profile by design: the evidence for traits other than ambition, training, style and income-driven adjustment is thin. NOT SCORED ON PURPOSE: the 22 September 1892 killing of his wife Paz Pardo de Tavera and mother-in-law Juliana Gorricho (documented by Matibag, VERA Files and the Ocampo pieces; he was acquitted by the Seine assize court in February 1893 and told to leave Paris, and the trial turned on jealousy, alleged infidelity and racial arguments) and the earlier domestic violence recorded in the trial: no attribute honestly measures this, the rubric forbids reading a diagnosis or fixed disposition into it, and any score drawn from it would be either misleading or a modern psychological label. Recommended for the lead: decide whether the public profile should carry a factual, non-trait note about it. Also unscored: the 1896 arrest, 1898-99 diplomatic missions and his brother's pardon (thinly sourced, dates vary), the Rizal friendship, and prizes as evidence. CONFLICTS NOT ADJUDICATED: birth date (23, 24 or 25 October 1857; only the year is used); number of medals in 1884 (three or four first-class, 'first gold medal'); date of the shooting (22 or 23 September 1892) and of the verdict (7 or 8 February 1893). Ocampo's crime-of-passion columns, the Inquirer 'Amok' piece and the National Historical Commission birth-date report were read but are not cited. Not opened or blocked: Britannica (403), Museo del Prado (403), Asia Tatler and Manila Bulletin (403), the Real Academia de la Historia biography (JavaScript page), NCCA page (not resolved). SELF-CALIBRATION: all five rows lowered at least once, none raised (see handback).
